newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia reminds Japan of own extremists.
newsitem.headline: Australia reminds Japan of own extremists.

text.p: Australia reminded Japan on Thursday that it had extremists of its own after a newspaper report that a politician's anti-Asian statements would hurt relations between Australia and Asia.
"I remind Japan that we have difficulties with some aspects and elements of their more extreme organisations," Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"And ... I acknowledge also: they are a democracy with freedom of speech. So is Australia."
Fischer was reacting to the latest international fall-out from the anti-immigration comments of populist independent politician Pauline Hanson, elected to parliament last year.

The Australian Financial Review, a national daily, on Wednesday quoted an unnamed Japanese official who linked Hanson's immigration debate to Australia's membership of the Asia-European Meeting (ASEM), an international forum.
The newspaper interpreted the remarks, by a senior adviser to Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, as casting doubt on Japan's support for Australian membership of ASEM.
But Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said later that he had sought and received assurances from Japan that it still backed Australia's application for membership.
Fischer refused to name any Japanese extremist group.
"One extreme group has a very unreformed view with regard to World War Two," he said.
"I don't like that," he added, without elaborating.
Japan's reluctance to fully acknowledge its role in World War Two has stirred complaints in Australia, some of whose soldiers were treated atrociously as prisoners of the Japanese.
Japan has been Australia's biggest trading partner since the 1960s.
